items.title: docs: give four README claims a source, a rule, or a deletion
items.body:
Four claims on the public page could not be checked by a reader. This page argues that the project reports what it finds, including what is unflattering. A claim it cannot back costs more here than in an ordinary repository, because the page's credibility is the deliverable.

Each of the four now names what it rests on. Where a claim could not be supported it was removed rather than made vaguer.

Nothing in `src/` or `analysis/` changed. No new video was measured.

---

## 1. The comparison to other detectors had no citation

**Was:** "Other published detectors are measured on these same clips. They report F1 in the low nineties."

This was the load bearing sentence on the whole page. It is what tells a reader the project is behind the state of the art. It had no source, and the range it gave does not exist.

**Now:** a table of four papers, each one read in full, with authors, year, venue and a link.

| who | year | where | F1 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Drutarovsky and Fogelton | 2014 | ECCV workshops, Springer LNCS 8927 | 82.0% |
| Fogelton and Benesova | 2016 | Computer Vision and Image Understanding 148 | 91.6% |
| Soukupova and Cech | 2016 | Czech Technical University report CTU-CMP-2016-05 | 95.2% |
| Fogelton and Benesova | 2018 | Computer Vision and Image Understanding 176 to 177 | 91.3% |
| **this app** | 2026 | this page | 84.6% |

Three things this changes beyond adding a source.

- **"Low nineties" was picking the middle of a spread and hiding both ends.** The real range is about 82% to about 95%. The oldest published result, from the people who made the clips, is 82.0%, which is **below** this app.
- **The 2014 paper prints no F1.** It prints precision 79.0% and recall 85.27%. The 82.0% was worked out from those two numbers, and the page says so rather than passing it off as printed.
- **The comparison is not level, and the benchmark's own author says so.** Fogelton scores each eye separately, so his blink total for these clips is 804 and not 408, and he counts a fast double blink as one. Soukupova and Cech report the best point on their own curve, chosen on the test data itself. Fogelton writes on his own site that comparing across papers is "not valid". That is now quoted on the page.

The page also warns that some published scores on these clips are near 98%, and that those are measured **per frame** rather than per blink. A reader who searches will find them. Saying out loud that they are a different test is itself worth publishing.

Only four papers are listed, because only four were read in full. Several other reported scores could be found only quoted inside somebody else's summary table. Those are not on the page.

## 2. "45 of the 53" was true only at this project's own tolerance

**Was:** "45 of the 53 land on top of a real blink rather than on an open eye, and half of them are 3 frames long or shorter."

**Now:** 38 of the 53, printed first, with its rule beside it. Take the detection exactly as the app reported it, widen nothing, and ask whether it shares at least one frame with a blink the human marked. A reader can check that against the clips' own annotation files with no preamble.

45 is given beside it with its own rule: widen the detection by four frames at each end first. The page says which of the two is the flattering number and why. That four frame slack exists to stop a **correct** detection being punished for disagreeing about an edge. Reusing it to decide what a **wrong** detection sat on is a different act, so it does not transfer for free.

Two further corrections in the same paragraph.

- **"Half of them are 3 frames long or shorter" was wrong.** Counting from the detection's first frame to its last, both included, it is 41 of 53. The counting rule is now stated.
- **8 of the 53 are more than four frames from any real blink.** That count is identical under both rules, and it is the one the argument actually rests on. It is now on the page.

The point being made survives the stricter reading. Most false alarms are one blink counted twice, not a blink imagined from nothing.

## 3. The 2.7% downsampling figure had no saved artifact

Regenerated from the existing corpus. Every per clip reading reproduces the earlier private run exactly. The number survives. Three things the page said about it did not.

- **The sign was missing, and it is positive.** Blink strength went **up** by 2.7%. Averaging neighbouring pixels removes more noise than signal. Reading "changed by 2.7%" as a small loss understated how flat the result is.
- **"A quarter of its size" did not match the number.** A quarter of the pixels is the x2 shrink, which is +2.3%. The 2.7% is the x4 shrink: a quarter of the width and a quarter of the height, so one pixel in sixteen.
- **The video was not shrunk. The eye boxes were.** And this measures the pixels, not the app. It rules out a picture too small to contain a blink. It does not show that the app's own eyelid measurement is resolution proof. The page no longer lets a reader take the second claim.

The page also now says the eight clips disagree: five rose, two fell a little, one did not move.

## 4. "Lost its opening one" claimed a count that is not recoverable

**Was:** "A third clip made exactly fifty detections and lost its opening one too."

The other numbers in that story imply two, not one. Neither is knowable. The capped export is the only surviving record of that run, and it holds fifty rows whatever number was cut from the front of it. The corrected run is a different build, so its detection count cannot be subtracted to recover the answer.

**Now** the page says only what is certain, in the wording already merged into `src/core/constants.ts` so the two agree: the rows that clip lost were false alarms and not blinks the human had marked, so no recall figure changes. The certainty comes from the clip being scored as finding the same 36 blinks in both runs.

---

## What makes these reproducible

Two scripts and their saved output, in `docs/evidence/2026-08-09/`.

| file | what it settles |
| --- | --- |
| `scripts/checks/false_positive_overlap.py` | the 38, the 45, the 41 and the 8, each with its rule printed beside it |
| `scripts/checks/resolution_snr.py` | the 2.7%, its sign, and every per clip reading behind it |
| `tables/false_positive_overlap.txt` | saved output of the first |
| `tables/resolution_snr.txt` and `.json` | saved output of the second |

Both take their paths as command line arguments, so neither carries a path off anybody's machine. That makes them the exception to the evidence folder's "edit the path at the top" note, and the folder README now says so.

`resolution_snr.py` decodes only a small crop around the eyes, so all eight clips take about 15 seconds. It only reads and writes nothing into the corpus.

**A number collision, now documented in the evidence README.** `tables/eyeblink8_false_positives.csv` has exactly 45 data rows, because the **first** run made 45 false alarms in total. The README's 45 is a different quantity from the **corrected** run. Anyone checking the claim by counting those rows would appear to confirm it for the wrong reason.

## One extra change

The page said Eyeblink8 is "71,354 frames in total" with no attribution. The dataset owner's page says 70,992 annotated frames, and the 2014 paper says over 82,600. The count is now attributed to the annotation files that came with the clips, which is where 71,354 comes from, and the page notes that other sources give other totals.

## Left alone deliberately, for you to decide

`docs/eyeblink8-result.txt` still carries two of the corrected claims, at lines 66 to 67 and 75 to 77:

- "which made exactly 50 detections and lost its first one"
- "45 of the 53 invented blinks sit on top of a real blink, and half of them are 3 frames long or shorter"

The brief scoped this change to `README.md` and `docs/evidence/`, so they were not touched. That file is linked from the README, so the repository now states two things two ways. **This is worth a follow up, and it is a one line decision rather than a measurement.**

## Gates

`npm run lint`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test` (442), `npm run e2e` (7), `npm run format:check`. In `analysis`: `ruff check .` and `pytest` (61 passed, 2 skipped). The evidence folder's own privacy check still prints `0`, so no byte above 127 was added.

Not merged, as asked.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)


---

# Adversarial review, second pass (commit `395caee`)

A second session re-checked every number on the page, recomputed several
from the raw corpus without importing any project code, and re-ran both
new evidence scripts.

## What held up

- **Fix 2 reproduced exactly.** An independent reimplementation (own `.tag`
  parser, own `.blinks.csv` parser, own greedy one-to-one matcher) gives
  338 of 408, recall 82.8%, precision 86.4%, F1 84.6%, 53 false alarms, **38**
  strict, **45** with tolerance, **41** three frames or shorter, **8** more than
  four frames away. The per-clip table and the seven tolerance-only frame
  ranges match the committed artifact line for line.
- **Fix 3 reproduced exactly.** `resolution_snr.py` re-run against the corpus
  regenerates `resolution_snr.txt` and `resolution_snr.json` **byte for byte**.
  The +2.71% average, and the five up / two down / one flat split, both check
  out.
- **Fix 4 held up.** `27122013_152435_cam` scores 36 true positives in both
  runs, and its first-run export holds exactly 50 detections. The wording
  agrees with `src/core/constants.ts`.
- Also re-verified: 55 of 70 misses contain a fully closed frame (78.6%),
  the shortest annotated blink is 4 frames, the evidence folder is 42 files
  and 291 KB, and `eyeblink8_false_positives.csv` really does have 45 rows.

## What did not hold up, and is now fixed

**1. The frame total was attributed to the wrong thing.** The page said
71,354 came from "the rows of the annotation files". It does not. The rows
number **70,992**, which is also the figure the dataset's own publishers print.
71,354 is the highest frame number in each file plus one, summed over the
eight clips. The rule is now stated, and both numbers are on the page.

**2. "The other three print F1 themselves" is false.** The Soukupova report
prints precision 94.3% and recall 96.2% and no F1 at all. Its 95.2% was
computed, exactly like the 2014 figure. Every F1 in the table now carries
its own provenance line.

**3. "Only those four were read in full" is not supportable.** The 2014, 2016
and 2018 papers are all paywalled with no open access version. The 91.6% and
91.3% are real and correct, but they come from Fogelton's own results table
at blinkingmatters.com, not from the papers. The 2014 numbers are second hand
from a 2017 paper. The page now says which is which.

**4. A claim that quietly flattered this project.** The page said published
scores near 98% on these clips "are measured per frame, not per blink", so
they could not be compared. That is false. **Al-gawwam and Benaissa, Information
2018, 9, 93** report precision 96.65% and recall 98.78% on Eyeblink8, evaluated
per blink. That paragraph is deleted and the paper is now **in the table at
97.7%**. The published spread on the page therefore moves from "about 82% to
about 95%" to **"about 82% to about 98%"**, which is less flattering and correct.

**5. One explanation was stated as a finding.** The reason the blink got
slightly stronger at lower resolution is now labelled as an explanation
offered, not something the check measured.

Also corrected: the Soukupova report is a thesis with Cech as advisor, "LNCS"
is spelled out, and the page now says on its own face that
`docs/eyeblink8-result.txt` still carries two superseded sentences.

## Is the page more or less flattering than before this pass?

**Less.** The top of the published range rose from 95% to 98%, the excuse for
ignoring the near-98% results is gone, three citations are now marked as
unread or second hand, and one explanation was downgraded to a guess. Nothing
was softened in this project's favour.

## Still waiting on the owner

`docs/eyeblink8-result.txt` (lines 66-67 and 75-77) remains out of scope and
still disagrees with the README. The README now admits this in public, which
contains the damage, but it does not remove it.

## Gates, re-run in full after the change

`lint`, `typecheck`, `test` (442), `e2e` (7), `format:check`; `ruff check .`
and `pytest` (61 passed, 2 skipped) in `analysis`. Both new evidence scripts
pass `ruff` cleanly on their own. Still not merged.

items.title: docs: drop the stale hardcoded test count from README
items.body:
The README said `pytest  # 233 tests`. The suite is at **291**, so the comment
had drifted by 58 tests.

Rather than write 291 and let it rot again, this drops the count:
`pytest  # full suite`.

## Why not just update the number

Test counts change on almost every PR — four of today's alone moved it. A
number that is wrong by 58 is worse than no number, because a reader who runs
`pytest` and sees a different figure has no way to tell whether they are
looking at documentation rot or a broken install.

Worth distinguishing from the other numbers in this README, which are staying.
`2,561-parameter MLP`, the MAE table, the fitted coefficients — those are
*claims about results*. They should be pinned precisely, and if they go stale
that is a signal something real changed and needs re-measuring. A test count is
incidental bookkeeping that changes for reasons nobody needs to be told about,
so pinning it only guarantees rot.

Verified while here: `2,561` is still exactly right
(`sum(p.numel() for p in FinishTimePredictor().parameters())`), and the
coverage floor line was already corrected to 97 in #83.

Docs only.

items.title: Publish the maths corpus, and make the README a kit rather than a log
items.body:
The maths mid-train corpus is now on the Hub at
[`chrishayuk/v11-mathonly-midtrain-corpus`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/chrishayuk/v11-mathonly-midtrain-corpus),
under the same content-addressed identity the catalog registered (`ff7bf26b…`).
The catalog copy still needs a key; this one does not, which is the difference
between a video someone can follow and one they can only watch.

The entrypoint deliberately still rebuilds at seed 90. The published copy is a
citable artifact and a reference to diff against, not a change to how workers get
their data.

## `training/publish_corpus_hf.py`

Four refusals, each for a failure that has already happened somewhere here:
publishing bytes that are not the registered corpus; hashing the corpus where it
lives (`training/data/` holds two corpora and the validation rows, and the
identity is over a *directory* — in place it hashes to `655400a5…`); silently
replacing published bytes; and describing the corpus from a file instead of from
the corpus.

That last one is why every number in the card is measured at publish time. After
the push it re-downloads what the Hub serves into a clean directory and recomputes
the identity.

## What measuring it turned up

**`datasets.json` had drifted from the bytes it describes.** `replay_tokens`
1,521,190 → 1,521,089 and `total_rows` 96,889 → 96,894 were the pre-determinism
build's figures. Its `generator.note` also still described the streaming-shuffle
non-determinism as current, after the seeded-stride fix landed. Both corrected.

**The shared validation set is 97.2% stories.** Both trainers identify replay rows
as `len(ids) > 40`, a proxy for "came from TinyStories", and 213 of the 90,000
narrative drill rows exceed it — so 20 of the 710 rows in `shared_val_710.jsonl`
are arithmetic drill items. Held out of training, so not leakage, but a figure
reported as "story replay NLL" is measured on 690 stories and 20 sums. Both arms
score the identical file, so the paired result is unaffected. Recorded rather than
fixed: changing the split would change that file's sha and make every completed
run incomparable. Flagging it as a decision to revisit before the remaining seeds
run.

## README

Six runnable steps up front, then the depth, then the production material below a
divider.

Its own quick start was tested from a fresh clone and **failed the first time** —
`hf download --local-dir` leaves a `.cache/` tree in the target even with
`--include`, so the corpus root hashed to `a9d67ca6…`. Nothing errors; training
runs happily either way, which is exactly why it needed catching.

`training/fetch_published.py` now does that step as a PEP 723 script like
everything else here, because the heredoc it replaced assumed torch was already
installed and this repo's whole promise is that nothing needs installing.

Clone → fetch → smoke mid-train verified end to end. The smoke run's pre-midtrain
val NLL comes out at 1.5893, the same number the results table quotes.

The status section was stale in a way that mattered: it listed the maths mid-train
as still to run and Act 4 as the long pole, and both have since happened.

## Also in here

`/clear` in the REPL, which was already written and is documented by the new
README, so the two had to land together. `3J` clears the scrollback as well as the
screen — without it a "cleared" frame is one scroll away from showing the takes
that did not work.

items.title: Synchronize the documentation with the current research frontier
items.body:
Presentation-layer only. Six files.

The sixth file, `scripts/reproduce.sh`, is a **comment-only** correction to the
local reproduction contract: no executable command in it changed.

Original scope note: **No mathematics changes**, and no
certificate identity moves.

The entry-point documents described a frontier that ended around P126/P129.
Everything from T130 onward — determinism, the closed map, slack and budget
analysis, T145, C146, C147 — and both gap-word classifications existed **only**
in `docs/theorem-status.md`. A reader arriving here could not have learned what
the current mathematical state is.

## Current-state prose corrected

**`README.md`** — reorganized around the mathematical hierarchy instead of the
order results were obtained: the recurrence and the open conjecture · what is
proved · the current structural reduction · the exhaustive computational
frontier · formal verification · reproducibility · where to read next.

The old claim table had grown by accretion and duplicated the ledger. It is
replaced by a compact proved-results table plus the T130→C147 reduction
narrative, with the ledger kept as the single authority.

**One correction is a factual error, not staleness.** The README claimed the
Lean development *does not* formalize the finite-start theorem. It does —
`Conjecture.finite_start` proves `m < (c+3)(3c+5)` with a clean axiom audit, and
`Conjecture.chain_length_bound` machine-checks the arithmetic core of T145. The
document was **understating its own verification**. The genuine limits are now
stated instead: growth bounds, all-period exclusion, and the two-counter /
expanding-window reduction remain unformalized.

Reproduction now matches what actually runs: CI described by capability rather
than a job count (including the cross-platform determinism gate and the arXiv
reproducibility build), `lake build --wfail` replaced by the `lake env lean`
invocation CI uses, and the fast-check list updated from an old subset to
include the gap-word verifiers.

K18/K19 appear in their own section as exhaustive computation with the scope
caution attached. Certificate hashes are deliberately **not** duplicated —
`docs/theorem-status.md` remains the single source.

**`docs/future-directions/future-directions-safe-map.md`** — its closing "do
next" targets asked for a chain argument that has since been built, so they were
stale. It now records the collapse (search → forced continuation → closed orbit
→ budget control → one expanding recurrence against a moving window) and names
**C147 as the actual unresolved problem**. K18/K19 are placed as instrumentation
for that problem, not progress toward it.

**`supplement/README.md`** — two claim-to-evidence rows for K18/K19 pointing at
the verifiers and the module split, following the file's existing convention of
not carrying long hashes.

C146 is stated as **unboundedness** throughout, never divergence.

## Visuals regenerated

**`assets/readme-hero.svg`** — regenerated, not patched. Content is now the four
evidence classes the project actually distinguishes (open · proved · exhaustive
computation · verified), recurrence kept visually central, computational card
explicitly labelled *not a theorem*. Layout follows the lessons from the earlier
hero-clipping work: taller cards, wider margins, no filters, and `Inter` dropped
from the font stack because GitHub lacks it and the fallback metrics shifted the
text. Inspected **rendered** at README width on light and dark pages, not only
parsed. Fully self-contained — no external fonts, images, or network refs.

**`audit/theorem-dependency.md`** — the graph gains the determinism spine T130 →
C147 as one readable chain, not every ledger row. K18/K19 attach with dashed
edges in the computational class and deliberately carry **no outgoing edge into
the open branches**: they are results, not logical prerequisites, and drawing
them as dependencies would misrepresent what rests on what. The open-branch
fan-ins are rewritten with Mermaid `&` chaining to fit the per-file length gate —
same edge set, different spelling.

Two pre-existing defects fixed while validating: `L103` was referenced by three
edges but never declared or classified (rendering unlabelled and uncoloured);
and `C46` is not a numbered claim at all but the conclusion of K13 together with
T46, so it is renamed rather than left impersonating a corollary.

## Historical records intentionally preserved

Untouched, because they are point-in-time records and rewriting them to look
current would destroy their value: `audit/evidence-manifest.md`,
`audit/release-readiness.md`, `audit/fresh-proof-review.md`,
`audit/opus-pr2-audit.md`, `audit/opus-reconciliation-verification.md`,
`audit/continuation-*.md`, `audit/scoped-post-freeze-band.md`, all nine
`docs/research-logs/*`, and `manuscript/arxiv/*` (deliberately narrow scope, and
CI gates its PDF reproducibility).

`audit/tail-123-142.md` was already current to C147 and its filename is
deliberately retained so published links keep resolving — left alone.

## Mathematics and certificate identities unchanged

`docs/theorem-status.md`, `independent/`, `certificates/`, `data/`, `lean/`,
`manuscript/`, and `.github/` are **provably untouched** — the diff against the base
contains no path under any of them. No theorem introduced or strengthened, no
bound changed, no computational evidence reinterpreted as proof.

`scripts/reproduce.sh` **is** touched, but no executable command in it changed:
stripping comments and blank lines before and after gives the identical
`sha256 7b8a2bdbf126d0d1db6b9f43da84da0aeaf7dd15c06312c62f0a5f5b2cbfc6b4`, and the
line-by-line executable diff is empty. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is unchanged at
blob `81e2636b`.

## No new quantitative figure

Considered and **rejected**. The strongest candidate was the continuation
collapse, but that is three numbers — 2,706 → 342 → 74 — which the compact table
already conveys exactly. A bar chart of three values teaches nothing further,
and a generator plus data plumbing would add maintenance surface for no
comprehension gain. The bar was set high deliberately; this did not clear it.

Relatedly, no stale-reference detector was added: the canonical K18/K19 values
appear as claims in exactly one file, so there is no duplication to police, and
this PR was written to keep it that way.

## Deferred

**Manuscript revision** — new chapters/sections for T130–C147 and K18/K19,
derived from the current proof sources, under separate mathematical-writing
review. `manuscript/*.md` is living but stops at P129; bringing it current is new
mathematical exposition rather than synchronization, so it is out of scope here.

## Validation

`git diff --check` clean · link checker passes (203 relative links, 498 inline
path spans, all resolve) · hero parses as XML and was visually inspected
rendered · every README asset path resolves · every theorem/K reference in every
touched file exists in the ledger · README Lean claims checked against the actual
Lean declarations and axiom audit, in both directions · every listed
reproduction command verified present in `reproduce.sh` or `ci.yml` ·
`bash -n scripts/reproduce.sh` passes · all touched files within the per-file
length gate.



---

## Review corrections (commit `5bf157e`)

Independent review caught two overclaims, both now fixed.

**1. CI trigger.** The README said CI runs on "every push and pull request on the
research branch". False: the workflow's `push` trigger is scoped to `main`, so a
plain push to a research branch runs nothing. This is precisely the mistake that
would let someone believe a research-branch commit had been checked when it had
not. Corrected to state that runs come from pull requests or manual dispatch,
with pushes to `main` automatic.

**2. Reproduction equivalence.** The README said `scripts/reproduce.sh` "runs the
same checks in the same order as CI". The order is right; the equivalence is not.
One host cannot supply the Ubuntu/Windows matrix, and therefore cannot supply the
cross-platform K18/K19 byte-determinism comparison that gives those certificates
their identity. CI also adds documentation-link and TeX structure checks and the
hosted paper-reproducibility environment. Both the README and the same stale
claim on line 2 of `scripts/reproduce.sh` are corrected.

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` was **not** changed to make either statement true.

|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2 | **`P=2`** at `0.09067` | all identically zero |
| 2 | 3 | **`P=3`** at `0.00694` | all identically zero |
| 3 | 4 | **`P=4`** at `0.00213` | `P=5` live at `10×` behind |
| 4 | 5 | **`P=5`** at `0.0001–0.0003` | all identically zero |

`d = 1` was the place it was most likely to break — a lattice has no junctions in the 2-D sense, since a "vertex" separating two sectors is just a wall. Had it failed there the honest claim would have been `d >= 2`.

## What a 4-D tessellation is made of

Codimension counting predicts four tiers where 3-D has three. All four are occupied (`P = 5`, two independent seed sets):

| valence | locus | run A | run B | falloff |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | domain interior | `0.579` | `0.579` | — |
| 2 | 3-D wall | `0.314` | `0.333` | `1.7–1.8×` |
| 3 | 2-D surface | `0.096` | `0.078` | `3.3–4.3×` |
| 4 | 1-D line | `0.0115` | `0.0104` | `7.4–8.3×` |
| 5 | **point vertex** | `0.00028` | `0.00010` | `41–107×` |

The falloff **accelerates** — point vertices are the scarcest structure by a widening margin.

**Are vertices scarcer at higher `d` because structure fails, or because points are small?** Mostly the second. Raw peak density drops `300–900×` from `d=1` to `d=4`, but a point is a vanishing fraction of a `d`-volume regardless and should scale like `(3/L)^d` on geometry alone. Dividing that out leaves a residual of **`3–8×`, not `300×`**, not even monotone. So **4-D point vertices form perfectly well and are simply geometrically scarce.**

## The texture guard is dimension-blind too

Same defect class as `distinct >= 3`, found the same way. A cell is wall if any of its `3^d − 1` neighbours differs, and that ring grows exponentially, so `domain_scale` falls with dimension at fixed physical domain size: 2-D at `5.14` and 4-D at `2.44` hold domains of `19.5` and `16.2` lattice units — comparable structures, opposite sides of the `2.5` cut.

`domain_diameter` reports the width directly. The property that earns it: **pure noise reads `1.0` in 2-D, 3-D and 4-D alike.** Its known failure direction is pinned rather than hidden — slabs over-read by about a factor of `d`. **Nothing switches over to it**, so no published reading changes underneath itself.

## Two disclosures

**The corrected guard is what makes `d = 4` readable at all** — `P=5`'s raw scale of `2.44` is below the published floor. The guard commit precedes the run and is derived from interior-fraction geometry rather than fitted, but an instrument licensing the result its author predicted is worth stating plainly.

**One published number was wrong and is corrected in `cffb18f`.** The first run gave `0.000278`; the in-experiment run at independent seeds gives `0.000097`. The ranking reproduced exactly; the density did not. The seed sets agree within 20% down to the line tier and diverge `2.8×` at the vertex — where the counting runs out, at 30–90 cells. All downstream figures were widened to ranges rather than the one number being patched.

---

# Part 2 — the README

**2137 → 160 lines.** It had become a hundred chronological experiment writeups, a 250-line module inventory and the full operational manual, with no way to find out what the repo claims.

Split by reader. **Nothing deleted** — 124 of 127 headings preserved verbatim, the three exceptions being intro sections deliberately rewritten:

| file | contents |
|---|---|
| `README.md` | what this is, the central result as a figure, load-bearing verdicts, what would refute it, quickstart |
| `Docs/Experiment_Log.md` | the chronological record + roadmap |
| `Docs/Usage.md` | CLI, agents, server, WebSocket, browser toys, module-by-module layout |

The results table carries the negatives on purpose — that capacity does **not** drive the palette selection, that the optimum's route was measuring the dictionary, and that `2/3` of the robustness re-scoring predictions failed.

## The figure

Four relaxed sector fields at `P = 2…5` with full-palette junction cells circled — `P=3` has them, the others don't. Generated by `tools/make_figures.py` from `n3_junction_scale.relaxed`, the same relaxation the published measurements use, so it cannot drift from the numbers. Verified byte-identical on re-run. Light and dark variants from a validated categorical palette stepped per surface — selected, not auto-flipped — served via `<picture>`.

Panels label junction **counts**, not densities: each shows one field while the published density is a three-trial average, and quoting the single-field number beside a different one in the docs would invite the reader to think one is wrong.

## The table was audited, and four rows overstated their experiments

Compressing ~100 experiments into seven rows is where overstatement creeps in, so every row was checked against its source (`46cd507`):

- **"Rivals are identically zero"** was false in 3-D, where `P=5` is live. `Junction_Selection.md` said so *on the same branch* — the summary contradicted the document it was summarising.
- **The area law is 2-D**, and the gap is `1.04`, not "exactly one dimension".
- **"The capacity law transplants"** claimed more than is settled. The eviction *condition* transplants; `crossing.py` states plainly that a substrate-independent `κ` is **not settled**.
- **"Three published claims turned out unevidenced"** was wrong by a factor of three — the three NOT EXERCISED verdicts are three *sweeps of one claim* (§2's gap), not three claims. Reframed from "1/3 held" to "2/3 failed", the same fact stated so the reader learns the blind spot was *narrower* than feared.

Also `geometric (Plateau's law)` → `codimension counting`, since Plateau's trivalent vertex is the `d=2` instance, not the general mechanism.

---

## Honest scope

Wherever rivals are identically zero this is **categorical**, not a robustness result: no perturbation could have changed those rankings. That's stronger than robustness and it's a different claim.

The `d=4` arm is the weakest of the four — ~1.5 domains per axis against 3.7 in the plane, and the `P=6,7` zeros can't be distinguished from under-sampling. **`d = 5` is unreachable by this route**: its point tier would sit near `1e-6`. That's a measurement ceiling, not evidence, and answering it needs a different instrument — sampling junctions directly rather than scanning every lattice cell.

## Verification

**1255 tests pass.** Two pre-existing `exp` overflow warnings in the Hopfield substrate, unrelated. The `d = 4` arm is opt-in (`--with-4d`, ~60 min) so the default run stays affordable.

Branch was restarted from `main` after #101 merged, so this is new work on top of the merged history.

items.body:
Closes the measurement defect found while running the #1021 Windows leg.

## The defect

Both inference servers bind IPv4 only, but `localhost` resolves to `::1` first on Windows and the
IPv6 connect has to time out before the client falls back — **~2.1 s of dead wait on every request**.
It never errors, so no artifact looks wrong: the run completes, reports zero errors, and produces a
clean-looking report.

Because `driver.py` loops requests until the burst deadline, the stall did not *slow* the bursts, it
**emptied** them. Every Windows run served **45 requests instead of ~350**, leaving each 20 s burst
**~85 % idle** — so the harness compared a nearly-idle window against the idle baseline and reported
the difference as contention.

Ollama's own accounting makes it provable:

| | via `localhost` | via `127.0.0.1` |
|---|---:|---:|
| Wall clock / request | 2.388 s | **0.271 s** |
| Ollama's own `total_duration` | 0.308 s | 0.255 s |
| prompt / gen tokens | 143.3 / 9.0 | 143.3 / 9.0 |

Same tokens, same inference time, 2.1 s of nothing in between.

## Blast radius

**This invalidates every Windows row of the #782 results table.** All five prior Windows artifacts
carry the identical signature — `localhost` endpoint, exactly 45 requests, ~2.3 s/request — including
`vulkan-qwen14b` (1.49×) and its `rep2` (2.48×), i.e. **the swing that motivated #1016 and #1021**.

That swing was not p99 instability. It was two nearly-idle windows being compared. Re-run under load,
the same Vulkan cell is a stable **2.50× [2.49–2.55]** across five runs.

## Changes

- `measure_windows.ps1`: default `-BaseUrl` → `127.0.0.1`; an explicit `localhost` now warns. The
  runbook itself instructed passing `-BaseUrl http://localhost:...`, so a corrected default alone
  would not protect anyone following it.
- `tools/gpu_contention/README.md`: corrected command, the IPv6-stall explanation, and the
  `Δ p95`-over-`Δ p99` guidance (#1019) marked **conditional** — it was drawn from a quantized 30 fps
  clock, and under full burst load on a 240 fps client the ordering reverses: p99 is the stable
  statistic there (spreads 0.18× and 0.06× against 1.61× and 1.50× effects), p95 the noisy one.
- `docs/ai-provider-evaluation.md`: same corrected command.
- `CHANGELOG.md`: `### Fixed` entry under `[Unreleased]`.

## Verification

Full Windows leg re-run on `earth` (RTX 5080, driver 610.62) after the fix — 5 runs per backend,
zero errors, **zero analyzer warnings**, all ten runs at one 4.16 ms idle cadence:

| Metric | CUDA (Ollama) | Vulkan (b10107, Ollama-matched) |
|---|---:|---:|
| p99 ratio | 2.61× [2.48–2.66] | 2.50× [2.49–2.55] |
| Δ p95 | 4.38 ms [1.86–6.35] | 4.38 ms [3.20–5.67] |
| Requests / run | **351** | **535** |

Request counts now match the Linux leg's operating point (373 / 540), which is the check that the
fix actually restored the load. Full results and reading in
https://github.com/fighters-legacy/fighters-legacy/issues/1021#issuecomment-5081548469.

No code paths outside the harness are touched; nothing here runs in CI.

items.title: Score FlowVQA degree questions; add max_outdegree
items.body:
## Problem

The M1 coverage harness tested for `"in-degree"` / `"in degree"`, but FlowVQA writes it as **one word** — `"indegree"`. The branch never fired, so **449 indegree questions** fell straight through to `continue` and went unscored. A further **101 outdegree questions** had no graph-tool function at all — spec §7.2 lists only `max_indegree`.

Net effect: the reported 98.8% silently excluded 12.5% of the topological set, including the subtype the tool handles worst.

## Changes

- `graph_tool.py`: add `max_outdegree`, computed over the DiGraph so a decision's parallel Yes/No edges into one target count once — matching `edge_count`'s existing convention. It scores 101/101 against gold, which confirms that convention is what FlowVQA expects.
- `tools/parser_coverage.py`: match FlowVQA's one-word phrasing, and test degree **before** `edge_count`, since these questions mention "incoming/outgoing edges" in their preamble. `edge_count` still scores 1172/1207, unchanged by the reorder.
- `tests/test_graph_tool.py`: cover `max_outdegree` against the fixture (D branches to E and F).
- `README.md`: corrected results table with per-subtype denominators, plus the test-count fix (was "14 tests", now 16 — it was already understated at 15 before this change).

## Results

| subtype | accuracy | scored |
|---|---|---|
| node_count | 100.0% | 1207/1207 |
| **max_outdegree** | **100.0%** | **101/101** |
| shortest_path | 99.6% | 822/825 |
| direct_predecessor | 99.1% | 766/773 |
| direct_successor | 98.4% | 801/814 |
| edge_count | 97.1% | 1172/1207 |
| **max_indegree** | **95.1%** | **427/449** |
| **overall** | **98.5%** | **5296/5376** |

Coverage goes from 4826 to **5376 of 5516** topological questions (87.5% → 97.5%).

**The headline moves down, 98.8% → 98.5%.** That's the point: `max_indegree` at 95.1% is now the weakest subtype and was previously invisible. A number covering 97.5% of the set is more defensible in the report than a higher one that drops its worst category.

## Verification

- 16/16 tests pass
- Harness re-run against the full `train_full.json` (1319 records)

## Not addressed

- `max_indegree`'s 22 failures aren't error-analysed yet
- The 129 label-unresolved questions remain the other known gap (likely the same duplicate-label root cause as `edge_count`)

items.body:
Writes up today's two free probes on the box and corrects last night's distillation write-up, which was never committed.

## New: `docs/research/width-and-capacity-probes.md`

Two probes, both chosen to pick the one variable the next paid run should change — after `regression-and-next-steps.md` closed both branches of the previous decision tree (P9 dropped when P8 tied, P10 taken and failed its gate).

**1. Search width is affordable.** `top_k` 64 -> 128 at n=128 costs **1.24x per self-play game** against a 2x pass threshold, no stall. Discharges R6 of `regression-and-next-steps.md` §3.3. Configs added as `run_configurations/blokus_width_topk{64,128}.json`. Also verified in code that width is visible at the root: Gumbel picks its 32 considered actions by Gumbel-top-k over the whole `top_k` window, so a rank-100 action can now enter the tree.

**2. Capacity still does not bind, now on external teacher data** — but the honest reason is that the design cannot resolve an effect this size. `xl` beat `large` by 0.039 nats held-out CE, which nominally clears P8's pre-registered 0.03 threshold. The noise floor — same net, same data, same split, weights rerolled — is **0.050**, and the replicate was the best arm of the three. Without that arm this reads as a false positive worth GBP 100-130.

**3. The methodological finding, which outranks both probes.** Run-to-run variation in this pipeline is ~0.050 nats held-out CE and ~0.022 weighted ladder. §4 applies that honestly to results already written down: the learning-rate, corpus-mix, data-volume and v2-over-v1 effects survive; capacity and the auxiliary heads were never resolvable; and N4/N5's reading that the reply head "clears the noise floor" should be retracted.

## Corrected: `docs/research/distillation-recipe-findings.md`

Four corrections, the first of which is the important one:

- **"The remaining route to level 9 is RL from v3" was wrong**, and written without reading the RL history. That has been tried three times for ~$125 and <=0 external gain, and §5 of the regression review explicitly recommends against a fourth with the current operator. Corrected to: RL with a *changed* operator, since the fixed point is a property of the operator and not of the starting net.
- **The v2-vs-v1 question is answered** — v2 wins by +0.060 weighted (0.339 vs 0.279), ~2.7x the floor. Both single-corpus arms sit below the 0.419 that v2-plus-20%-v1 reaches, so the corpora are complementary.
- **Capacity scoped to imitation.** All four capacity tests are supervised, where the ceiling is the teacher, so a tie is the expected reading either way. "Stop testing net size" overreached; it is a bad buy today, not a closed question for RL.
- **Noise floor recorded** against the results table, so no reader takes a sub-0.022 delta as a measurement.

## What a reviewer should check

- The retraction in §4 is the claim with the widest blast radius — it changes how the N4/N5 rows in `docs/plans/supervised-network-improvements.md` must be re-run. Those rows are **not** edited here (one concern per PR).
- These capacity CE numbers are not comparable to the blended runs in the distillation doc: the re-run dropped `--v1-mix` after a first attempt hit its own 2-hour-per-arm timeout. Only `large`-vs-`xl` within the run is meaningful, and §5 says so.
- Unrelated drift spotted, not fixed here: `docs/research/README.md`'s Contents table has not tracked new docs for a while (it is missing the plateau, regression, technique-review and corpus-quality docs, among others).

Raw artefacts stay on the box; provenance paths are listed in §5.

items.title: feat(ci): invariant 13 — every scoreboard row declares its sample size
items.body:
Closes the **last actionable candidate** in
[docs/CONVENTIONS-LEDGER.md](docs/CONVENTIONS-LEDGER.md), and fixes five stale
surfaces found by re-checking the ones this cycle touched.

## Invariant 13

Each row of the results table in `evals/results/RESULTS.md` must fill its
`Samples` cell. A lift from one run is typographically identical to a lift from
ten, and this repo has been burned twice: a **+0.07** retracted when the set grew
15 → 49, and a **+0.40** corrected to **+0.39** by a second run. Neither looked
uncertain on the page.

Like invariant 10 it is a **regression guard** with no incident of its own — all
10 rows pass today. It catches the *next* row added without an `n`, which is the
cheap moment; the expensive one is after the number has been quoted.

**Shape-driven, not position-driven.** It finds the table by its `Samples`
**header** and checks that column in every data row beneath, so a renamed or
dropped column fails closed rather than passing over zero rows — the drift a
hardcoded column index sails straight past.

**Process substitution, not a pipe.** A `| while` runs the loop in a subshell, so
every `v13=1` set inside it would be discarded on exit: a gate that finds
offenders, prints them, and still exits 0.

### Watched to fail first

| Case | Exit | Output |
|---|---|---|
| Blanked `Samples` cell | 1 | `NO SAMPLE SIZE: …:20 — "Audit (14 hard snippets)"` |
| `Samples` column renamed | 1 | `SCOPE EMPTY` (tables **and** rows) |
| Scoreboard file absent | 0 | `SKIPPED` — not assumed |
| Clean tree | 0 | `ok (10 scoreboard rows)` |

## Five stale surfaces fixed

- **`README.md` said "Eleven invariants"** — missed by the earlier sweep because
  its grep was case-sensitive. Its coverage list also omitted four of them
  (rules-file indexing, single `[Unreleased]`, `LAST-VERIFIED` pairing, rendered
  assets); it now names all thirteen areas instead of trailing off after six.
- **`docs/MAINTENANCE.md`** had its structure-row *count* bumped to 12 while its
  parenthetical *list* kept the old contents — a count that agrees with the
  script while the prose beside it does not.
- **`docs/INDEX.md`** had no route to the render procedure added a day earlier: a
  documented procedure with no front-door row, which is `RELEASING.md` §2b's
  class applied to the index rather than the README.
- **`RELEASING.md`**'s social-preview step described re-rendering by hand with no
  mention that invariant 12 now enforces the commit-both half.
- **`docs/ROADMAP.md`**'s open-tasks header still read *as of 2026-08-01*, listed
  the Samples guard as open, and called §2b "the only other candidate".

## One correction, recorded rather than hidden

"4 more enforced inside the eval runners" was briefly changed to **3**, on the
assumption the Samples guard had come from that set. It did not — it came from
the *gateable but not gated* table, and the runner-enforced set is still 4.
Caught by re-reading the ledger and reverted before it propagated.

  residual stale count outside the CHANGELOG's historical entries

items.title: docs(perf): dispatch is free — codegen at MapStruct parity, type-specialized subclass declined
items.body:
## What

Carries the `BRIDGE_FN` codegen-perf measurement to a conclusion **across two CI runs**, and corrects `docs/perf-mapstruct-comparison.md` to the reproducible truth. This is the "benchmark, then decide" gate on the roadmap's codegen-parity item — the answer is **parity is already achieved and the remaining optimization is not worth building.**

## Findings (two CI runs, same branch, all four call shapes each)

Forward ratio (codegen `BRIDGE.read` ÷ MapStruct):

| Tier | Run 1 | Run 2 | Verdict |
|------|------:|------:|---|
| flat | 1.065× | 1.072× | **stable ~1.07×** |
| nested | 1.043× | 1.424× | **JMH-noisy baseline — no single figure** |
| deep | 1.185× | 1.137× | **stable ~1.15×** |

Dispatch shape (forward, ns) — reproducible across both runs:

- **`BRIDGE_FN` (one hop) sits at the `static forward` (zero hop) floor** — run 2 flat has them identical at 3.183. The JIT inlines the monomorphic hop; it is the fastest passable value there is.
- **The full-lattice `BRIDGE.read` runs 0–0.3 ns above that floor** — tied on flat/deep, ~0.3 ns above on run-2 nested and *outside* the tight ±0.04–0.09 error bands. The lattice wrapper is a small, occasionally measurable tax on the composable value specifically — not "free everywhere" (an earlier single-run revision overstated this; the confirmation run corrected it).

## The decision: **do not build step 2**

The type-specialized subclass would remove only the ≤0.3 ns wrapper tax, and only from `BRIDGE.read` — adopters who want the floor already have `BRIDGE_FN`. ~100 LOC of `BridgeProcessor` complexity to shave ≤0.3 ns off one of two already-shipped call shapes. Declined. The only real gap vs MapStruct is ~6–7 ns of generated-**body** work on the deep tier (`static forward` is ~1.15× too, so it isn't dispatch), adopter-gated on a real deep-tier hot loop.

## Changes

- **Benchmarks**: added `nested_*_bridgefn_forward` and `deep_*_bridgefn_forward` (flat already existed) so all four call shapes compare on each run.
- **`docs/perf-mapstruct-comparison.md`**: two-run results tables, a two-run dispatch table, corrected headline/dispatch-section/remediation-statuses/bottom-line. `BRIDGE_FN` = floor; wrapper tax = 0–0.3 ns; nested = noisy; step 2 declined.
- **No production code.** `BRIDGE_FN` already ships (#182); codegen is at parity as-is.

## Deliberately out of scope

The public README / `benchmarks/README.md` still carry the prior canonical run's ratios (1.15×/1.56×/2.01×). The two runs here confirm deep ~1.15× (matches the README's headline "tie") and flat ~1.07× (better than the README's 1.56×), but nested is too noisy to publish a figure. A public-numbers refresh — updating flat, keeping deep, characterizing nested as noisy — is a sensible follow-up but out of scope for this measurement PR.

items.body:
## Summary

Fixes #1. Three commits, one per priority tier:

- `fix: repair invalid YAML frontmatter and unify version metadata` (P0): the `code-review` and `tdd` skill descriptions contained a mid-scalar `: ` that broke strict YAML parsing while the MCP server's regex-based reader silently accepted it; quoted both. Synced version across `package.json`, `plugin.json`, and `mcp-server.js` (which now reads it from `package.json` instead of a hardcoded literal). Rewrote `smoke-test.mjs` to validate every skill's frontmatter as real YAML, assert an exact `prompts/list` match against the discovered skill set, and diff every `prompts/get` response against its `SKILL.md` file byte-for-byte.
- `fix: tighten mutation-confirmation boundaries and resolve skill ownership conflicts` (P1): `repo-secure` now requires explicit confirmation before enabling any GitHub setting (not just branch protection) and checks code-scanning eligibility first; `architecture-diagram` now distinguishes show/save/commit instead of defaulting to commit; `repo-ship` split into two conditional paths (commit-by-intent vs new-repo creation) with separate Done checklists, and `release-versioning`'s trigger no longer overlaps ordinary commits; `explain-plainly` no longer creates a glossary unless an existing repo convention (owned by `domain-modeling`) authorizes it; `project-groundwork`'s undefined "project memory" term now resolves to the repository's actual decision-recording convention, or states plainly when none exists.
